cards.definition: A dramatic genre ending in the downfall or death of the protagonist, often caused by a fatal flaw.
A central character of high status whose fatal flaw leads to their downfall and death.
The fatal flaw or error in judgement of a tragic hero that causes their downfall.
Excessive pride or self-confidence in a tragic hero, often the cause of their destruction.
The inevitable punishment or downfall that follows a tragic hero's pride or crimes.
A dramatic speech delivered alone on stage, revealing a character's innermost thoughts to the audience.
A remark made by a character heard by the audience but not by other characters on stage.
When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension or dark humour.
A recurring element — image, symbol or idea — that carries thematic significance throughout a text.
The emotional release felt by the audience at the end of a tragedy, purging pity and fear.
The tragic hero; a brave general whose unchecked ambition and susceptibility to manipulation lead to tyranny and death.
Macbeth's wife; initially ruthless and manipulative, she plans Duncan's murder but is later destroyed by guilt.
The virtuous, trusting King of Scotland; his murder by Macbeth represents the destruction of divine order.
Duncan's son and rightful heir; he flees after his father's murder and later leads the force to defeat Macbeth.
Macbeth's loyal friend; the witches prophesy his descendants will be kings. Macbeth has him murdered out of fear.
A Scottish nobleman loyal to Duncan; he eventually kills Macbeth, fulfilling the witches' prophecy.
Three supernatural figures who deliver equivocal prophecies that tempt and mislead Macbeth to his destruction.
A Scottish nobleman who acts as a messenger, conveying news of war and betrayal throughout the play.
The goddess of witchcraft; she rebukes the witches for interfering with Macbeth without her authority.
A comic figure providing relief after Duncan's murder; his speech on equivocation reinforces a key theme.
The dangerous desire for power that drives Macbeth and Lady Macbeth; Shakespeare presents it as morally corrupting.
Both Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are destroyed by guilt — Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost; Lady Macbeth sleepwalks.
The witches, ghost and visions blur the line between reality and imagination, driving characters to destruction.
Nothing is as it seems — 'Fair is foul and foul is fair'; characters are repeatedly deceived by surfaces.
Contrasts good kingship (Duncan, Malcolm) with tyranny (Macbeth); linked to the Jacobean concept of divine right.
Lady Macbeth and Macbeth both wrestle with distorted ideas of what it means to be a man; violence is equated with strength.
Macbeth's treachery against Duncan, a kinsman and king, is the ultimate betrayal and sets the tragedy in motion.
The corrupting nature of power is central; Macbeth's seizure of the crown destroys him morally and politically.
The witches' prophecies raise the question of whether Macbeth's downfall was inevitable or the result of his own choices.
Duncan's murder creates chaos in both the natural and political world; order is only restored with Macbeth's death.

cards.keyword: Fair is foul, and foul is fair
cards.definition: The witches establish the theme of appearance vs reality from the outset — nothing in the play is what it seems.
Macbeth asks darkness to hide his murderous ambitions from heaven, showing early moral awareness of his intentions.
Lady Macbeth asks the spirits to remove her femininity so she can commit murder without conscience.

cards.keyword: Is this a dagger which I see before me?
cards.definition: Macbeth's hallucination before the murder shows how guilt and ambition are already disturbing his mental state.

cards.keyword: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood clean?
cards.definition: Macbeth recognises the enormity of his crime — no amount of water can remove his guilt.
Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking reveals her psychological collapse; she imagines blood she cannot wash away.
The witches announce Macbeth's arrival, showing his transformation from hero to villain in their eyes.
Macbeth's nihilistic soliloquy on the meaninglessness of life after Lady Macbeth's death.

cards.keyword: None of woman born shall harm Macbeth
cards.definition: A witches' prophecy that gives Macbeth false security — undone by Macduff's caesarean birth.

cards.keyword: Too full o' the milk of human kindness
cards.definition: Lady Macbeth believes Macbeth lacks the ruthlessness needed to seize the crown — she must drive him on.
Macbeth was written c.1606 during the reign of James I; Shakespeare's themes directly engaged with contemporary concerns.
The belief that kings were appointed by God; murdering Duncan was therefore an act against God as well as man.
A Catholic attempt to blow up Parliament; themes of treason and equivocation resonated strongly with audiences.
James I wrote Daemonologie (1597) on witchcraft; the witches in Macbeth would have genuinely terrified Jacobean audiences.
A hierarchical order from God to animals; disrupting it by murdering a king caused chaos in the natural world.
The killing of a king; considered the most heinous crime in Jacobean society, damning the murderer to hell.
A doctrine of telling half-truths; debated at the Gunpowder Plot trials and central to the witches' misleading prophecies.
A society dominated by male authority; Lady Macbeth must reject her femininity to gain power, reflecting Jacobean norms.
Shakespeare drew on Aristotle's theory — a noble protagonist falls from grace through hamartia and hubris.
James was patron of Shakespeare's company and a descendant of Banquo; the play flatters him directly.
A work of fiction shorter than a novel but longer than a short story, often focused on one theme.
A narrative where characters and events represent broader moral or political meanings beyond the surface story.
Intended to teach a moral lesson; A Christmas Carol is explicitly didactic, designed to change readers' attitudes.
A literary style using darkness, decay and the supernatural to create fear; used in descriptions of the spirits.
An appeal to the emotions of the reader; Dickens uses Tiny Tim and the Cratchits to generate sympathy.
The term Dickens uses for chapters, evoking music and the festive theme — there are five staves in the novella.
The narrator has access to all characters' thoughts and addresses the reader directly, creating intimacy.
A recurring element; fire, light, cold and warmth recur throughout to symbolise generosity and moral state.
Marley's ghost and the heavy chain foreshadow Scrooge's fate if he does not change.
A list of words or phrases piled together for emphasis, e.g. Dickens' description of Scrooge's character.
The protagonist; a cold-hearted miser transformed into a generous benefactor through the visitations of three spirits.
Scrooge's deceased business partner; condemned to wander in chains forged by his own greed, he warns Scrooge.
Represents memory and conscience; shows Scrooge the warmth and loss of his earlier years to stir his emotions.
A jolly giant representing generosity; shows Scrooge the joy he is missing and the poverty of the Cratchits.

cards.keyword: Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
cards.definition: A silent, dark, hooded figure representing death and consequence; shows Scrooge his own unmourned death.
Scrooge's underpaid clerk; represents the deserving poor — hardworking, grateful and devoted to his family.
Bob's disabled son; a symbol of innocence and the vulnerable poor. His death in the alternative future shocks Scrooge.
Scrooge's cheerful nephew; embodies the generosity and warmth of Christmas spirit that Scrooge has rejected.
Scrooge's former fiancée; she breaks off their engagement when she realises he has replaced her with money.
Scrooge's beloved sister and Fred's mother; her early death is a source of Scrooge's emotional withdrawal from the world.
Dickens argues the wealthy have a moral duty to help the poor; Scrooge's transformation enacts this message.
Dickens exposes the brutal poverty of Victorian London, contrasting it with the wealth of the upper classes.
The novella shows that change is possible for even the most selfish individual if they confront their past.
Christmas represents generosity, compassion and community; Scrooge's journey is about reconnecting with these values.
Scrooge's obsession with money has left him isolated; Dickens critiques the capitalist values of Victorian society.
The Cratchits and Fred's household represent the warmth and happiness that come from human connection.
The Ghost of Christmas Past uses memory to reconnect Scrooge with his emotions and guilt.
The three ghosts take Scrooge through past, present and future, showing that it is not too late to change.
The two allegorical children beneath the Ghost of Christmas Present; Dickens presents them as society's greatest dangers.
Marley's chains and Scrooge's unmourned death warn of the consequences of a life spent in selfishness.
Marley's warning to Scrooge: the business of life is human welfare, not commercial profit.
The narrator's opening description of Scrooge establishes his cold, unyielding character through extended metaphor.
Scrooge echoes Victorian attitudes toward the poor, exposing the cruel indifference of the wealthy.
Tiny Tim's blessing closes the novella; an expression of universal goodwill embodying the Christmas spirit Scrooge has found.

cards.keyword: I will honour Christmas in my heart
cards.definition: Scrooge's vow to carry the lessons of past, present and future always — the climax of his transformation.
A simile capturing Scrooge's deliberate isolation from society — closed, sealed and self-protective.

cards.keyword: The chains he forged in life
cards.definition: Marley's chain, made of cash-boxes and ledgers, metaphorically represents how greed imprisons and punishes its owner.

cards.keyword: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.
cards.definition: The Ghost's allegorical children — a direct appeal by Dickens for readers to act on social reform.
Dickens' accumulation of adjectives condemns Scrooge's character comprehensively from the outset.
Belle's accusation that Scrooge has chosen money over love — the moment that defines his emotional isolation.
The reign of Queen Victoria (1837–1901); rapid industrialisation created huge wealth alongside extreme urban poverty.
The growth of factories created a new industrial poor; Dickens witnessed and wrote against the resulting deprivation.
Malthus argued the poor should not be helped as they would overpopulate; echoed in Scrooge's 'surplus population' speech.
Forced the poor into workhouses rather than providing outdoor relief; Dickens was furious about its cruelty.
Institutions where the destitute had to work for food and shelter in degrading conditions.
Children as young as five worked in mines and factories; Dickens campaigned against it throughout his career.
At 12, Dickens worked in a blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt; this shaped his empathy for the poor.
The Victorian belief that the market should be left alone and the state should not intervene to help the poor.
Voluntary schools for destitute children; Dickens supported them and they inform his concern for ignorance in the novella.
Written in six weeks and published in December 1843; Dickens wanted it to reach as wide an audience as possible.
A literary form intended to be performed; An Inspector Calls uses theatrical conventions for political effect.
A form of drama using characters to represent moral values; AIC has similarities in its didactic, allegorical structure.
A tightly constructed drama building to a revelation; AIC subverts this by leaving questions unresolved.
Birling's praise of the Titanic and dismissal of war are key examples — the 1945 audience knew he was wrong.
Priestley's instructions on setting and lighting carry significant meaning, e.g. the Inspector's commanding entrance.
Background information given at the start to establish character and situation before the main action.
The resolution of the plot; AIC deliberately withholds a satisfying denouement to unsettle the audience.
The final telephone call is one of drama's most famous cliff-hangers, leaving the ending unresolved.
Technique used for theatrical effect, such as the single set, real-time action or the Inspector's mysterious identity.
AIC can be read allegorically: the Inspector represents collective conscience; the Birlings represent capitalist society.
A mysterious, authoritative figure; may be supernatural — a moral force, a ghost or Priestley's socialist mouthpiece.
A pompous, self-made businessman; represents capitalist complacency and the arrogance of the upper-middle class.
Arthur's cold, snobbish wife; she refuses to accept responsibility and is the last to help Eva, making her the most culpable.
The Birlings' daughter; initially self-absorbed, she undergoes genuine moral growth and fully accepts responsibility.
The Birlings' troubled son; he impregnated Eva and stole from his father, but like Sheila he accepts responsibility.
Sheila's fiancé and son of a rival businessman; he had an affair with Eva/Daisy. His response is ambiguous and self-serving.
The dead girl; never seen, making her a symbol of all exploited working-class women rather than an individual.
The Birlings' maid; a minor character whose silent presence as a servant reinforces the household's class assumptions.
Birling begins confident and ends relieved nothing is 'real' — he has learned absolutely nothing from the Inspector's visit.
Sheila begins shallow and ends as the play's moral voice — Priestley presents the younger generation as capable of change.
The central theme; Priestley argues through the Inspector that we are all responsible for each other's welfare.
The rigid Edwardian class system is exposed as cruel and hypocritical; the Birlings exploit those below them.
Eva has no power as a working-class woman; Sheila's limited agency reflects women's position in 1912 society.
Birling embodies selfish capitalism; the Inspector voices Priestley's socialist belief in collective responsibility.
The younger Birlings (Sheila, Eric) are capable of change; the older generation (Arthur, Sybil) refuse to learn.
Each character bears partial responsibility for Eva's death; Priestley asks which characters the audience resembles.
The Inspector represents moral justice; whether real or supernatural, justice will eventually arrive.
The Birlings present themselves as respectable but their treatment of Eva reveals their moral bankruptcy.
The Birlings abuse their power over Eva at every stage; Priestley shows how the powerful exploit the vulnerable.
The play's real-time structure and 1912/1945 double setting make its warnings about consequence urgent and unavoidable.

cards.keyword: We are members of one body
cards.definition: The Inspector's final speech; a direct expression of Priestley's socialist belief in collective moral responsibility.
The Inspector prophesies WWI and WWII; gives the play urgent political resonance for its 1945 audience.

cards.keyword: A man has to mind his own business
cards.definition: Birling's capitalist philosophy is immediately undermined by the Inspector's arrival — Priestley presents it as dangerously wrong.
Dramatic irony; Birling's confidence signals to the 1945 audience that his judgement cannot be trusted on anything.

cards.keyword: You're beginning to pretend nothing much has happened
cards.definition: Sheila challenges her parents' refusal to learn — she represents the younger generation's capacity for change.
Sybil's dismissal of Eva reveals her class prejudice and total refusal to see Eva as a fellow human being.

cards.keyword: These girls aren't cheap labour — they're people
cards.definition: Sheila's moral awakening; she recognises Eva's humanity where her father saw only economic units.
Birling's offer of money shows he still thinks wealth can solve moral problems; he has learned nothing.

cards.keyword: Each of you helped to kill her
cards.definition: The Inspector's collective accusation links each character's action in a chain of responsibility leading to Eva's death.

cards.keyword: Not the kind of father a chap could go to when he's in trouble
cards.definition: Eric exposes Birling's failure as a father; his authority was built on fear, not love or genuine care.
A socialist writer from Bradford; he served in WWI and wrote AIC in 1945 after WWII, having witnessed the cost of inequality.
Set just before WWI in a period of apparent stability; the audience knows the complacency of characters like Birling is fatal.
First performed in 1945; audiences had just lived through WWII and were voting Labour — the play's message felt timely.
Characterised by rigid class divisions, limited rights for women and workers, and entrenched deference to the wealthy.
Established in 1945; Priestley strongly supported it — AIC was written partly to build public support for collective responsibility.
Women were campaigning for the vote in 1912; Eva's powerlessness reflects the vulnerability of unenfranchised women.
Workers were organising for better pay; Birling's sacking of Eva for strike action reflects real class tensions of the era.
Birling confidently predicts no war; the audience knows millions died — Priestley uses this to undermine capitalist confidence.
In Edwardian Britain, your birth determined your life chances; Priestley saw this as morally indefensible.
WWII required collective sacrifice; Priestley argued this spirit of community should continue into peacetime reconstruction.
A turn or shift in argument, tone or perspective within a poem, often at a key structural moment.
A metre with ten syllables per line in an unstressed-stressed pattern; associated with formality and tradition.
Poetry without a regular rhyme scheme or metre, allowing for a natural, conversational or fragmented tone.
When a sentence or phrase runs over from one line or stanza to the next without a pause.
A deliberate pause within a line of poetry, often shown by punctuation, creating emphasis or tension.
Words that almost rhyme but don't quite; used to create dissonance and unease, e.g. in Owen's poetry.
A poem in the voice of a single speaker, often revealing character through what they say and omit.
A poem of mourning or lamentation, typically written in response to death or loss.
Two consecutive lines of poetry that rhyme, often used to conclude or summarise a point.
A grouped set of lines within a poem, equivalent to a paragraph in prose.
Nature is shown as overwhelming or indifferent to human ambition; seen in Exposure and Storm on the Island.
The capacity of individuals or states to dominate, destroy or control others; seen in Ozymandias and The Emigrée.
Internal and external struggles — war, identity, memory — explored across all 15 poems in the cluster.
How the past is preserved, distorted or mourned; central to Kamikaze, Poppies and War Photographer.
The experience of losing people, places, identity or innocence; present in Poppies, Remains and Kamikaze.
How individuals or communities define themselves under pressure; explored in The Emigrée and Checking Out Me History.
War achieves nothing and destroys human potential; central to Exposure, Remains and Bayonet Charge.
The extension of power by conquest; critiqued in Ozymandias and Checking Out Me History.
Psychological damage from violent experience; central to Remains, Bayonet Charge and War Photographer.
The passing of time and its effect on power, memory and nature; a linking concept across many poems.
The shattered statue symbolises how even the greatest human power is temporary; pride leads to inevitable decay.
The boastful inscription survives surrounded by nothing — a devastating irony that undermines the boast entirely.
Shelley uses a sonnet — associated with immortality — ironically; the form itself cannot preserve Ozymandias.
A traveller tells the narrator; the double remove distances the speaker, suggesting the story has become legend.
The hand that mocked them — the sculptor's art has outlasted the king's power; art may outlast empire.
Blake's repeated 'In every' creates a relentless rhythm, suggesting the inescapable, systematic nature of suffering.
'Chartered streets' and 'chartered Thames' — even nature has been commodified by commercial control.
'Marks of weakness, marks of woe' — both physical and spiritual; the city leaves visible signs of suffering on its people.
Child labourers whose suffering 'appalls' the Church — a religious institution complicit in exploitation.
Blake's metaphor for psychological oppression; people are imprisoned by their own acceptance of authority.
Armitage uses blunt, everyday language to capture a soldier's mindset and the psychological aftermath of killing.
The soldier relives the incident in the present tense, suggesting the trauma is ongoing and inescapable.
Lines overflow across stanzas, mimicking the uncontrollable nature of traumatic memory and intrusive thoughts.

cards.keyword: Remains — his bloody life in my bloody hands
cards.definition: The ambiguity of 'bloody' (literal and emphatic) captures both the physical reality and emotional burden of killing.
The looter's body 'tends to stay' — the soldier cannot escape the memory; PTSD is powerfully implied.
A mother's experience of a son leaving for war, told through the metaphor of Remembrance Sunday poppies.
Small, intimate details (blazer, sellotape) contrast with the enormity of loss; the personal within the political.
It is never stated the son has died; the ambiguity leaves the reader sharing the mother's uncertainty and anguish.
The lack of rigid structure mirrors the mother's emotional fragmentation; grief resists neat, ordered form.
The mother imagines her son as a free bird; hopeful yet painful, suggesting her inability to protect him.
Personification of wind as an enemy; nature, not the opposing army, is what kills the soldiers in Exposure.
'What are we doing here?' — Owen's repeated question emphasises the futility and purposelessness of soldiers' suffering.
The poem ends where it begins; the soldiers are no closer to relief — a structural image of hopelessness.
The repeated refrain; the true enemy is inaction and waiting, not the German guns — war as exposure, not heroism.
Owen uses unsatisfying half-rhymes (e.g. 'wire/war') to create dissonance, reflecting the discomfort of the trenches.
'King, honour, human dignity, etcetera' — abstractions that drove men to war become meaningless in the moment of terror.
The immediacy of present-tense verbs puts the reader in the soldier's terrified body, collapsing all distance.
The soldier becomes a 'hare' — a hunted animal. Hughes strips away his humanity to show how war dehumanises.
The sudden, abrupt verb; the soldier is ambushed by his own terror — thought is a liability in combat.
Three uneven stanzas mirror the soldier's stumbling, chaotic progress; form enacts the disorder of battle.
